source_text: Over 350 million people currently are chronically infected and are at high risk for progression to cirrhosis, liver failure, or cancer.

evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental data from photo-cross-linking and tandem affinity purification experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane transporter predominantly expressed in the liver.

claim: An N-terminal myristoylated peptide corresponding to amino acids 2–48 of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein effectively blocks both HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes.
source_text: An N-terminal myristoylated peptide corresponding to amino acids (aa) 2–48 of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein has been shown to effectively block both HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work (Barrera et al., 2005; Glebe et al., 2005; Gripon et al., 2005; Engelke et al., 2006; Schulze et al., 2010).

source_text: L-photo-leucine contains a photoactivatable diazirine ring.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the chemical structure of L-photo-leucine, which is established chemical knowledge.

claim: Irradiation of ultraviolet (UV) light at 365 nm induces a loss of nitrogen of the diazirine ring and yields a reactive carbene group with short half-life for covalent cross-linking at nearly zero distance.
source_text: Irradiation of ultraviolet (UV) light at 365 nm induces a loss of nitrogen of the diazirine ring and yields a reactive carbene group with short half-life for covalent cross-linking at nearly zero distance
evidence_reasoning: This describes the photochemical mechanism of diazirine activation, which is established knowledge supported by citation (Suchanek et al., 2005).

source_text: Primary hepatocytes isolated from treeshrews (Tupaia belangeri), the only species susceptible to human HBV infection other than humans and chimpanzees
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about Tupaia susceptibility to HBV, supported by citations (Su et al., 1987; Walter et al., 1996; Glebe et al., 2003).

source_text: the only species susceptible to human HBV infection other than humans and chimpanzees
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about HBV host range, supported by citations.

claim: Leu11 in the pre-S1 domain is 100% conserved among HBV genotypes.
source_text: Leu11 is 100% conserved among HBV genotypes
evidence_reasoning: This is based on sequence analysis data of HBV genotypes, representing established knowledge about HBV sequence conservation.

claim: The 14th residue of pre-S1 is a phenylalanine in most genotypes but a leucine in some HBV strains of genotypes F and G.
source_text: the 14th residue is a phenylalanine in most genotypes but a leucine in some HBV strains of genotypes F and G.
evidence_reasoning: This is based on sequence analysis data of different HBV genotypes.

claim: Changing phe14 to leucine (F14L) did not significantly affect the binding of HDV virion to primary Tupaia hepatocytes (PTHs).
source_text: Changing phe14 to leucine (F14L) did not significantly affect the binding of HDV virion to primary Tupaia hepatocytes (PTHs) (Figure 1B).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental binding assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: WTb inhibited HDV binding to PTHs with efficiency comparable to Myr-47/WT that is comprised of all natural amino acids.
source_text: WTb inhibited HDV binding to PTHs with efficiency comparable to Myr-47/WT that is comprised of all natural amino acids (Figure 1A,C).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental binding inhibition data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A peptide Myr-47/N9Kb (or N9Kb hereafter) similar to WTb but with an additional mutation at the ninth residue (N9K) did not block HDV binding to PTHs.
source_text: A peptide Myr-47/N9Kb (or N9Kb hereafter) similar to WTb but with an additional mutation at the ninth residue (N9K) did not block HDV binding to PTHs (Figure 1C).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental binding inhibition data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WTb but not N9Kb inhibited viral infection of HBV and HDV on PTHs.
source_text: WTb but not N9Kb inhibited viral infection of HBV and HDV on PTHs (Figure 1D).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental infection inhibition data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: N9Kb differs from WTb by only one amino acid but completely lost blocking activities.
source_text: N9Kb differs from WTb by only one amino acid but completely lost these blocking activities.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by the experimental data comparing WTb and N9Kb activities.

claim: WTb cross-linked with a glycoprotein of molecular weight at approximately 65 kDa in PTHs.
source_text: Cultured PTHs at 24–48 hr after isolation and plating were photo-cross-linked with 200 nM Myr-47/WTb (WTb) or Myr-47/N9Kb (N9Kb), followed by Streptavidin Dynal T1 beads precipitation and Western blot analysis using mAb 2D3. The protein cross-linked by WTb is sensitive to PNGase F treatment and shifted from ∼65 to ∼43 kDa.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental photo-cross-linking and Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The protein cross-linked by WTb is sensitive to PNGase F treatment and shifted from approximately 65 to approximately 43 kDa.
source_text: The protein cross-linked by WTb is sensitive to PNGase F treatment and shifted from ∼65 to ∼43 kDa.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental deglycosylation data shown in Figure 2A, indicating the protein is glycosylated.

claim: Non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT peptide (WT) but not its N9K mutant competed with 200 nM of WTb peptide for cross-linking with PTHs in a dose-dependent manner.
source_text: Non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT peptide (WT) but not its N9K mutant competed with 200 nM of WTb peptide for cross-linking with PTHs in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental competition assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The abundance of the target protein(s) in PTH cells decreased over time in culture.
source_text: The abundance of the target protein(s) in PTH cells decreased over time.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental time-course cross-linking data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: WTb cross-linked with a glycoprotein of molecular weight at approximately 60 kDa in primary human hepatocytes (PHH), which shifted to approximately 39 kDa upon PNGase F treatment.
source_text: WTb cross-linking with primary human hepatocytes (PHH). Frozen PHH cells were thawed and plated 1 day before cross-linking. With same procedure as in panel A, 200 nM WTb but not N9Kb cross-linked with a glycoprotein of molecular weight at ∼60 kDa, which shifted to ∼39 kDa upon PNGase F treatment.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental photo-cross-linking data in PHH shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The common protein hit identified by MS analysis of the approximately 65- and approximately 43-kDa bands cut from the WTb cross-linked sample was Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP).
source_text: The common protein hit identified by MS analysis of the ∼65- and ∼43-kDa bands cut from the WTb cross-linked sample was Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Two different tryptic peptide fragments were identified from both the approximately 65-kDa and approximately 43-kDa bands that matched to a protein homolog of human NTCP.
source_text: Two different tryptic peptide fragments, which were identified from both the ∼65-kDa and ∼43-kDa bands (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), matched to a protein homolog of human NTCP.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart.
source_text: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart
evidence_reasoning: This is based on sequence alignment analysis of tsNTCP and human NTCP.

claim: Tupaia NTCP has an insertion of 30 aa near its C-terminus compared to human NTCP.
source_text: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart and has an insertion of 30 aa near its C-terminus (Figure 2F).
evidence_reasoning: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: WTb but not N9Kb specifically cross-linked with hNTCP and tsNTCP expressed in 293T cells.
source_text: 293T cells transfected with an expression vector or plasmid containing cDNA of hNTCP or tsNTCP fused with a C9 tag at its C-terminus were cross-linked with 200 nM Myr-47/WTb or Myr-N9Kb similarly as in Figure 2A at 24 hr post-transfection.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental photo-cross-linking data in transfected cells shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WTb but not N9Kb bound to tsNTCP-EGFP expressed on the cell surface.
source_text: 293T cells transfected with tsNTCP-EGFP or a control hSDC2-EGFP (encoding human heparan sulfate proteoglycan core protein fused with EGFP at C-terminus) expression plasmid were incubated with WTb or N9Kb in the presence or absence of 200 nM non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT as indicated. Bound peptides were probed with PE-streptavidin and the colocalization of peptide and NTCP on cell surface was shown in the merged images.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FITC-pre-S1 peptide binding to Huh-7 cells was increased by hNTCP transfection.
source_text: 24 hr post-transfection with hNTCP or a control plasmid, the cells were stained with 200 nM FITC-pre-S1 (FITC-labeled lipopeptide corresponding to the N-terminal 59-amino acid of pre-S1). The binding was analyzed by flow cytometry.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Wild-type HDV but not HDV with a N9K mutation on its L protein showed increased binding to Huh-7 cells transfected with hNTCP.
source_text: Huh-7 cells, after 24 hr of transfection of indicated plasmids, were incubated with wild-type HDV or HDV with a N9K mutation on its L protein. Bound virions were quantified by qRT-PCR. The result is presented as fold changes of binding over the background virus binding to pcDNA6-transfected cells.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental virus binding data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of tsNTCP in PTHs inhibited HDV infection as indicated by reduced levels of HDV viral RNAs.
source_text: Infections of HDV and HBV in PTHs were inhibited by tsNTCP knockdown. Freshly isolated PTHs were transfected with siRNAs against tsNTCP or a control siRNA. 3 days later, 1 × 105 PTHs were inoculated with HDV, HBV, or control viruses AAV8-HBV and Lenti-VSV-G. For HDV and HBV, PTHs were infected at 500 and 100 genome equivalent copies per cell, respectively. The level of HDV viral RNAs in infected cells was quantified by qRT-PCR on 6 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental siRNA knockdown and infection data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knockdown of tsNTCP in PTHs did not affect VSV-G pseudotyped lentivirus infection.
source_text: For VSV-G control virus infection, recombinant lentivirus pseudotyped by VSV-G carrying a luciferase reporter was inoculated to PTHs 3 days after siRNA transfection. The luciferase activity was assessed on 6 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental control infection data shown in Figure 4A, demonstrating specificity of NTCP for HBV/HDV entry.

claim: Knockdown of tsNTCP in PTHs inhibited HBV infection as indicated by reduced levels of secreted viral antigens HBsAg and HBeAg.
source_text: For HBV infection, the kinetics of secreted viral antigens HBsAg and HBeAg were measured by ELISA. The medium was changed every 3 days.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental siRNA knockdown and HBV infection data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NTCP knockdown did not affect AAV8-HBV infection in PTHs.
source_text: For AAV8-HBV infection, PTHs were infected with a recombinant AAV8 carrying 1.05× overlength HBV genome. Secreted HBeAg was assessed on indicated days post-infection. The effect of tsNTCP silencing in all viral infections was independently evaluated with a total of four siRNAs against tsNTCP (see 'Materials and methods'). The data shown are the result of a representative siRNA out of the four tested.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental control infection data shown in Figure 4A, demonstrating that NTCP functions at the viral entry level.

claim: NTCP has no effect on post-entry steps of HBV infection.
source_text: This result shows that NTCP has no effect on post-entry steps of HBV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the AAV8-HBV control experiment data showing no effect of NTCP knockdown on AAV8-mediated HBV genome delivery.

claim: The NTCP mRNA level was low in HepaRG cells before induction but increased dramatically when the cells differentiated after induction.
source_text: The NTCP mRNA level was low in HepaRG cells before induction when examined on days 5 and 10 after initial plating, but increased dramatically when the cells differentiated after induction (Figure 4B, upper-left).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: About 70% HDV infection was reduced by hNTCP knockdown in differentiated HepaRG cells as indicated by decreased levels of HDV viral RNAs.
source_text: About 70% HDV infection was reduced by hNTCP knockdown as indicated by decreased levels of HDV viral RNAs (Figure 4B, upper-right).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental siRNA knockdown and HDV infection data in HepaRG cells shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HBV infection in differentiated HepaRG cells was inhibited by hNTCP knockdown as indicated by significantly reduced HBeAg and viral RNAs.
source_text: Similarly, HBV infection was also inhibited as indicated by significantly reduced HBeAg at multiple time points (Figure 4B, lower-left), as well as viral RNAs including the 3.5 kb RNA for HBV pre-C and pregenome RNA (pgRNA) and HBV total RNA (Figure 4B, lower-right) quantified at the end of the experiment.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental siRNA knockdown and HBV infection data in HepaRG cells shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of hNTCP significantly reduced HBV infection in PHHs.
source_text: Consistently, knockdown of hNTCP significantly reduced HBV infection, which was correlated with the NTCP mRNA knockdown efficiency. Both viral antigens and viral RNAs were decreased in cells transfected with hNTCP-specific siRNAs but not with the control siRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental siRNA knockdown and HBV infection data in PHHs shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NTCP is a common key cellular receptor component necessary for HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes.
source_text: Taken together, these data demonstrate NTCP as a common key cellular receptor component necessary for HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is inferred from the combined knockdown experiments in multiple cell types showing requirement of NTCP for infection.

claim: NTCP mRNA expression is low in human hepatocarcinoma cell lines that are not susceptible to HBV or HDV infection.
source_text: NTCP mRNA expression is low in human hepatocarcinoma cell lines that are not susceptible to HBV or HDV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The levels of NTCP mRNA in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells were about 10,000 times lower than that in primary human and Tupaia hepatocytes.
source_text: The levels of NTCP mRNA in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells were about 10,000 times lower than that in primary human and Tupaia hepatocytes (Figure 5A).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Transient transfection of hNTCP rendered Huh-7 cells susceptible to HDV infection.
source_text: 1 × 105 Huh-7 cells were transfected with 100 ng hNTCP/pcDNA6 or a vector control in 24-well plate and maintained in PMM, 24 hr after transfection, transfected cells were infected with HDV at 500 genome equivalent copies per cell. On 8 dpi, HDV delta antigen, which typically locates in nuclei, was stained with 4G5 antibody in green, nuclei were stained with DAPI in blue.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental transfection and infection data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HDV infection of hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells was blocked by HBV entry inhibitors including HBIG, Myr-59, and anti-HBsAg mAb 17B9.
source_text: Huh-7 cells transfected with hNTCP were infected with HDV similarly as in panel B in the presence or absence of HBV entry inhibitors: HBIG (hepatitis B immune globulin), Myr-59, and anti-HBsAg mAb, 17B9. 4G5 was used as an antibody control. HDV RNA copies of infected cells were quantified by real-time RT-PCR on 6 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental infection inhibition data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HDV viral RNAs in hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells increased over time after infection.
source_text: Huh-7 cells transfected with hNTCP were infected with HDV similarly as in panel B. The HDV viral RNAs in infected cells at indicated time points were quantified by real-time RT-PCR.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental time-course infection data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HDV infection of hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells increased with increasing multiplicities of genome equivalents.
source_text: With 100 ng hNTCP/pcDNA6, 1 × 105 Huh-7 cells were transfected, as in panel B. Transfected cells were infected with increasing mge of HDV as indicated. HDV delta antigen was detected as in panel B on 8 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental dose-response infection data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: HDV infection of Huh-7 cells increased with increasing levels of hNTCP transfection.
source_text: About 1 × 105 Huh-7 cells were transfected with a vector pcDNA6 or hNTCP/pcDNA6 at indicated amounts and cells were inoculated with 500 mge of HDV. HDV delta antigen was detected on 8 dpi as in panel B.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental dose-response transfection data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Transient transfection of hNTCP rendered HepG2 cells susceptible to HDV infection.
source_text: About 2 × 105 HepG2 cells were transiently transfected with 0.3 µg hNTCP/pcDNA6 or a vector control and maintained in PMM. Cells were infected at 500 mge with HDV 24 hr after transfection. On 8 dpi, HDV delta antigen in infected cells was stained with mAb 4G5 (left) and the HDV viral RNAs were determined by real time RT-PCR.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental transfection and infection data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HepG2 cells transiently transfected with either tsNTCP or hNTCP supported HBV infection as evidenced by continuous secretion of HBeAg over time and accumulation of HBV replicative intermediate viral RNAs in the infected cells.
source_text: HepG2 cells transiently transfected with either tsNTCP- or hNTCP-supported HBV infection as evidenced by continuous secretion of HBeAg over time and accumulation of HBV replicative intermediate viral RNAs in the infected cells.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental transfection and HBV infection data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The entry inhibitor Myr-59 blocked HBV infection of NTCP-transfected HepG2 cells.
source_text: The entry inhibitor Myr-59 blocked the infection
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental infection inhibition data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HepG2-hNTCP stable cells supported HBV infection as indicated by intracellular HBsAg expression.
source_text: HepG2-hNTCP stable cells or parental HepG2 cells were inoculated with HBV at 100 mge. On 9 dpi, intracellular HBsAg of infected cells on coverslips was stained with antibody 17B9 in green, and nuclei were stained with DAPI in blue.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HBV infection of HepG2-hNTCP cells resulted in secretion of HBeAg that was blocked by entry inhibitors.
source_text: The cells were infected with HBV at 100 mge in the presence or absence of entry inhibitors as indicated. The medium was changed every 2 days. Secreted HBeAg was measured at 3, 5, 7 dpi; each time point represents the level of newly synthesized HBeAg within every 2 days.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HBV infection efficiency of HepG2-hNTCP cells is correlated with the viral inoculum dose.
source_text: HBV infection efficiency is correlated with the viral inoculum dose. With increasing dose of HBV, 2 × 105 HepG2-hNTCP cells were infected as indicated. HBV RNAs in infected cells was examined on 10 dpi with real-time RT-PCR for the total HBV RNAs and the 3.5 kb transcripts.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental dose-response infection data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HBV cccDNA was detected in HepG2-hNTCP cells infected with HBV but not in parental HepG2 cells or in the presence of Myr-59.
source_text: HepaG2-hNTCP cells or HepG2 parental cells were infected with 100 mge of HBV in the presence or absence of Myr-59. HBV cccDNA was extracted from ∼ 2–3 × 106 infected cells on 7 dpi. Half of the extracted DNA of each sample was subjected to a 1.3% agarose gel and analyzed by Southern blotting.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental Southern blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HBV cccDNA levels in HepG2-hNTCP cells increased over time after infection.
source_text: HBV cccDNA (in panel E) was quantified at indicated time points post infection (see 'Materials and methods'). A dotted line indicates the background amplification.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental kinetic qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: HBV RNA copies in HepG2-hNTCP cells increased over time after infection.
source_text: HBV RNA copies (in panel F) in the infected cells were measured at indicated time points, data of similarly infected parental HepG2 cells on 9 dpi were also shown.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental kinetic qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: About 10% HepG2-NTCP cells were infected with HBV at multiplicities of genome equivalents (mge) of 100, which is comparable to the efficiency of HBV infection of PHHs.
source_text: As shown by intracellular staining of HBV core antigen (HBcAg) on day 8 post-infection, about 10% HepG2-NTCP cells were infected at multiplicities of genome equivalents (mge) of 100, which is comparable to the efficiency of HBV infection of PHHs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The level of secreted HBeAg from HepG2-NTCP appeared to be higher than that in PHHs from two donors.
source_text: The level of secreted HBeAg from HepG2-NTCP appeared to be higher than that in PHHs from two donors
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental ELISA comparison data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The levels of viral RNAs per nanogram of total cell RNA in HepG2-NTCP and PHHs are comparable.
source_text: whereas the levels of viral RNAs per nanogram of total cell RNA in both infected cell types are comparable (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental qRT-PCR comparison data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected HepG2-NTCP cells despite significant amount of HBeAg secretion.
source_text: The levels of viral DNA in the media resulted from the ongoing infection during days 4–13 post-infection were low (equivalent to ∼1% of input viral DNA copies) despite significant amount of HBeAg secretion during this period.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental viral DNA quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected PHHs.
source_text: Similarly, only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected PHHs (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, right).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental viral DNA quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs infected with culture medium collected from infected HepG2-NTCP cells.
source_text: In line with the low HBV viral DNA level in the medium inoculum, very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs on day 13 post-infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 5)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Crab-eating monkey (Macaca fascicularis) is not susceptible to HBV infection.
source_text: Crab-eating monkey (Macaca fascicularis) is not susceptible to HBV infection
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about HBV host range and species susceptibility.

claim: Monkey NTCP (mkNTCP) did not support pre-S1 binding or HDV infection when expressed in Huh-7 cells.
source_text: Huh-7 cells were transfected with plasmids encoding tsNTCP, hNTCP, mkNTCP, or NTCP mutants as indicated. The mutant NTCPs include hNTCP-bearing mutations of mkNTCP residues and mkNTCP-bearing mutations of human residues at indicated positions. The transfected cells were maintained in PMM for 24 hr and then either stained with 200 nM FITC-pre-S1 or infected with 500 mge HDV under the same experimental conditions as described in Figure 5B.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental binding and infection data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Replacing aa 157–165 of mkNTCP with human counterpart rendered mkNTCP an efficient receptor for pre-S1 binding and HDV infection.
source_text: Replacing aa 157–165 of mkNTCP with human counterpart rendered mkNTCP an efficient receptor for pre-S1 binding and HDV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis, binding, and infection data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All NTCP variants expressed comparable levels of NTCP on the cell surface.
source_text: All NTCP variants expressed comparable levels of NTCP. Huh-7 cells transfected as in panel A were biotinylated 24 hr after the transfection, then lysed and analyzed for cell surface NTCP expression (top), total NTCP expression (middle), and GAPDH (bottom), respectively.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Replacing aa 157–165 of mkNTCP with human counterpart rendered mkNTCP capable of supporting HBV infection.
source_text: HepG2 cells were transfected with plasmids encoding hNTCP, mkNTCP, or hNTCP variants bearing the indicated monkey residues, or mkNTCP variants with the indicated human residues. Transfected cells were maintained in PMM for 24 hr, and subsequently infected with HBV at 100 mge. HBeAg and HBV 3.5 kb RNA were assayed on 6 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental mutagenesis and HBV infection data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: NTCP (Slc10a1) is the founding member of the SLC10 family of solute carrier proteins.
source_text: NTCP (Slc10a1) is the founding member of the SLC10 family of solute carrier proteins.
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about NTCP classification and protein family membership.

claim: NTCP is a hepatic Na+ bile acid symporter and is responsible for cotransportation of sodium and bile acids across cellular membranes to maintain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids.
source_text: It is a hepatic Na+ bile acid symporter and is responsible for cotransportation of sodium and bile acids across cellular membranes to maintain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids
evidence_reasoning: This describes the established physiological function of NTCP, supported by citations (Hagenbuch and Meier, 1994; Stieger, 2011).

claim: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane glycoprotein presumed to span the cellular membrane up to 10 times with small extracellular loops.
source_text: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane glycoprotein presumed to span the cellular membrane up to 10 times with small extracellular loops
evidence_reasoning: This describes the structural properties of NTCP based on prior studies, supported by citations (Mareninova et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2011).

claim: NTCP is mainly expressed in the liver.
source_text: It is mainly expressed in the liver (Stieger, 2011), consistent with the liver tropism of HBV and HDV.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the tissue distribution of NTCP based on established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes.
source_text: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes (Stieger et al., 1994)
evidence_reasoning: This describes the subcellular localization of NTCP based on prior studies, supported by citation.

claim: The sinusoidal localization of NTCP fits well with its receptor role for blood-borne HBV and HDV.
source_text: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes (Stieger et al., 1994), a location that fits well with its receptor role for blood-borne HBV and HDV.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference connecting the known localization of NTCP to its proposed function as a viral receptor.

claim: HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate.
source_text: Whereas HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate (Schulze et al., 2007; Leistner et al., 2008)
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about the initial attachment mechanism of HBV, supported by citations.

claim: The interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific.
source_text: our data demonstrate that the interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the experimental data showing specific binding and functional interactions between NTCP and pre-S1.

claim: NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
source_text: NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing requirement of NTCP for infection and ability to confer susceptibility.

claim: NTCP expression rapidly decreased over time in cultured PTHs after isolation.
source_text: Consistent with previous reports on primary cultures of rat hepatocytes (Liang et al., 1993; Rippin et al., 2001), NTCP expression rapidly decreased over time in cultured PTHs after isolation.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and consistent with cited prior studies in rat hepatocytes.

claim: The decrease in NTCP expression over time may at least partially explain why primary hepatocytes typically remain susceptible to HBV infections in vitro for only a few days after isolation from liver tissues.
source_text: This may at least partially explain the observations that primary hepatocytes typically remain susceptible to HBV infections in vitro for only a few days after isolation from liver tissues (Gripon et al., 1988; Seeger et al., 2007).
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference connecting the observed decrease in NTCP expression to the known limited susceptibility window of primary hepatocytes, supported by citations.

claim: NTCP is functionally conserved in mammals.
source_text: NTCP is functionally conserved in mammalians
evidence_reasoning: This represents general knowledge about the evolutionary conservation of NTCP function across mammalian species.

claim: Protein sequences of NTCP vary among species.
source_text: but protein sequences of NTCP vary among species
evidence_reasoning: This is based on sequence comparison data and general knowledge about protein sequence variation across species.

claim: NTCP sequence variation among species is likely to contribute to the narrow species tropism of viral infection.
source_text: protein sequences of NTCP vary among species, which is likely to contribute to the narrow species tropism of viral infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference connecting NTCP sequence variation to the observed species specificity of HBV/HDV infection.

claim: Despite the high level of protein sequence homology between human and monkey NTCP, monkey NTCP did not support HBV and HDV infection.
source_text: Strikingly, despite the high level of protein sequence homology between human and monkey NTCP, the later did not support HBV and HDV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental infection data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Amino acids 157–165 of NTCP are critical determinants for pre-S1 binding and viral infections.
source_text: Replacing a small motif of aa 157–165 of mkNTCP with the corresponding hNTCP residues converted mkNTCP to a receptor for pre-S1 binding as well as HDV and HBV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from experimental mutagenesis data showing that this region is necessary and sufficient to confer receptor function.

claim: It remains to be determined if and how NTCP contributes to the species specificity of HDV and HBV infection in other species.
source_text: Further studies are warranted to determine if and how NTCP contributes to the species specificity of HDV and HBV infection in other species.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about future research directions based on the current findings.

claim: It remains to be determined if other molecule(s) additional to NTCP contributes to the cellular entry of HBV and/or HDV as a coreceptor(s) or receptor component(s).
source_text: It also remains to be determined if other molecule(s) additional to NTCP contributes to the cellular entry of HBV and/or HDV as a coreceptor(s) or receptor component(s)
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about the possibility of additional receptor components beyond NTCP.

claim: It remains to be determined if other host factors such as the microenvironment or architecture of hepatocytes in liver, or soluble blood components contribute to HBV and/or HDV infection.
source_text: and if other host factors such as the microenvironment or architecture of hepatocytes in liver, or soluble blood components like those that have been shown to involve in infections of other viruses (Shayakhmetov et al., 2005; Morizono et al., 2011), contribute to HBV and/or HDV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about potential additional host factors, drawing analogy from other viral systems cited.

claim: Expression and subcellular distribution of NTCP are precisely regulated under physiological conditions.
source_text: Expression and subcellular distribution of NTCP are precisely regulated under physiological conditions.
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about NTCP regulation in normal physiology.

claim: NTCP accounts for most, if not all, hepatic Na+-dependent bile acid transport.
source_text: NTCP accounts for most, if not all, hepatic Na+-dependent bile acid transport (Stieger, 2011).
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about NTCP's role in bile acid transport, supported by citation.

claim: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma.
source_text: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about NTCP expression in liver cancer, supported by citations (Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997; Zollner et al., 2005).

claim: NTCP expression is inversely correlated with the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis.
source_text: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma (Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997; Zollner et al., 2005) and the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis (Lee and Kim, 2007).
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about NTCP expression in liver disease, supported by citation.

claim: The newly discovered role of NTCP as an entry receptor for HBV and HDV raises interesting questions regarding its involvement in viral pathogenesis.
source_text: The newly discovered role of NTCP as an entry receptor for HBV and HDV raises interesting questions regarding its involvement in viral pathogenesis.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of the findings for understanding viral pathogenesis.

claim: Identification of NTCP as a functional receptor for HBV and HDV advances our understanding of their entry into host cells.
source_text: Identification of NTCP as a functional receptor for HBV and HDV advances our understanding of their entry into host cells
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about the significance of the findings for the field's understanding of viral entry.

claim: Identification of NTCP as a functional receptor may lead to new prevention and treatment strategies against HBV and HDV and related diseases.
source_text: Identification of NTCP as a functional receptor for HBV and HDV advances our understanding of their entry into host cells and may lead to new prevention and treatment strategies against these viruses and related diseases.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications of the findings.

claim: A Tupaia hepatocyte proteome database was established by deep sequencing of the transcriptome.
source_text: The tandem mass spectra were searched against a Tupaia hepatocyte protein database, which we had established by deep sequencing of the transcriptome (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence_reasoning: This describes a methodological achievement of the study, supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The Tupaia hepatocyte proteome database contains 91,479 protein sequences.
source_text: A total of 91,479 protein sequences were identified.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative result from the bioinformatics analysis of the Tupaia transcriptome.

claim: Major human hepatocyte protein classes are represented in the Tupaia hepatocytes proteome database generated in this study.
source_text: Major human hepatocyte protein classes are represented in the Tupaia hepatocytes proteome database generated in this study.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by Gene Ontology analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The peptide containing 4 aa of the 30 aa insertion unique to tsNTCP was one of the two peptides identified by the MS analysis at a high confidence level.
source_text: The peptide (TEETIPGTLGNSTH) containing 4 aa of this insertion (underlined) was one of the two peptides identified by the MS analysis at a high confidence level (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The control band cut from N9Kb cross-linked sample did not generate any hits on NTCP peptides.
source_text: The control band cut from N9Kb cross-linked sample did not generate any hits on any of these peptides.
evidence_reasoning: This is a negative control result from mass spectrometry analysis, demonstrating specificity of WTb cross-linking.

claim: HepaRG is the only cell line known to date to be susceptible to HBV and HDV infections upon differentiation into a mixture of hepatocyte-like and biliary-like cells.
source_text: Human hepatoma cell line HepaRG is the only cell line known to date to be susceptible to HBV and HDV infections upon differentiation into a mixture of hepatocyte-like and biliary-like cells (Gripon et al., 2002).
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about HepaRG cells as a model system, supported by citation.

claim: HepaRG differentiation requires a lengthy cell culture procedure, including maintaining undifferentiated cells for 2 weeks before induction, followed by induction with corticoids and DMSO for another 2–4 weeks.
source_text: HepaRG differentiation requires a lengthy cell culture procedure, including maintaining undifferentiated cells for 2 weeks before induction, followed by induction with corticoids and DMSO for another 2–4 weeks (Gripon et al., 2002).
evidence_reasoning: This describes the established protocol for HepaRG differentiation, supported by citation.

claim: The two photo-leucines were incorporated into the critical receptor-binding region of WTb without interfering with its receptor-binding activity.
source_text: Two photo-leucines were incorporated into the critical receptor-binding region of WTb without interfering with its receptor-binding activity, which allowed highly specific zero distance cross-linking of its direct binding partner(s) but not other neighboring molecules.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing that WTb retained binding and inhibitory activities comparable to the natural peptide.

claim: The covalent interaction between the WTb ligand and its partner(s) enabled a purification process under high-stringency conditions.
source_text: The covalent interaction between the WTb ligand and its partner(s) enabled a purification process under high-stringency conditions
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about the methodological advantage provided by the photo-cross-linking approach.

claim: Efficient isolation of the NTCP-WTb complex was achieved irrespective of the nature of the binding partner even though it is a membrane protein with multiple transmembrane domains.
source_text: and efficient isolation was achieved irrespective of the nature of the binding partner(s) even if it is a membrane protein(s) with multiple transmembrane domains, like NTCP identified here.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about the methodological success, supported by the successful identification of NTCP.

claim: Amino acids 9–15 of pre-S1 are known to be critical for viral infection.
source_text: two residues (leu11 and phe14) in a region (aa 9–15) known to be critical for viral infection (Schulze et al., 2010) were chosen for substitution with L-photo-leucine.
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about the functional importance of this region, supported by citation.

claim: Efficient HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells in vitro normally requires high dose of virus inoculums.
source_text: Efficient HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells in vitro normally requires high dose of virus inoculums
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about HBV infection requirements in vitro, supported by citations (Gripon et al., 1988; Gripon et al., 2002; Boehm et al., 2005).

claim: Only limited progeny viruses are produced after HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells.
source_text: and only limited progeny viruses are produced after infection (Gripon et al., 1988; Gripon et al., 2002; Boehm et al., 2005).
evidence_reasoning: This represents established knowledge about HBV replication in vitro, supported by citations.

claim: The majority of residual viruses from inocula were removed by changing the medium and washing during the first few days of infection.
source_text: As indicated by drastic decline of viral DNA level on day 4 post-infection, the majority of residual viruses from inocula were removed by changing the medium and washing during the first few days of infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental viral DNA quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Some host factors that are lacking in cell cultures might be needed for efficient viral particles formation or releasing.
source_text: It is reasonable to speculate that some host factors that are lacking in cell cultures might be needed for efficient viral particles formation or releasing
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement attempting to explain the low levels of progeny virus production in culture.

claim: Some cellular factors in cultures may hinder viral particle formation or release processes during infection.
source_text: or some cellular factors in cultures may hinder these processes during infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement offering an alternative explanation for low progeny virus production.

claim: Only very limited HBV infection occurred in PHHs inoculated with culture medium from infected HepG2-NTCP cells, which may be attributed to the low multiplicity of infection.
source_text: In line with the low HBV viral DNA level in the medium inoculum, very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs on day 13 post-infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 5), indicating that only very limited HBV infection might have occurred, which may be attributed to the low multiplicity of infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from experimental data showing low viral RNA levels in infected PHHs, attributed to low viral titer in the inoculum.
